Aside from the fact that this very clearly gives Microsoft an unneeded, unwanted and dangerous level of control over the computer that is supposed to be yours, there is also the fact that plenty of these patches have undesirable effects. For instance, the "upgrades" and "improvements" to the Windows Genuine Program (or whatever they're calling it these days) often ultimately just mean "this patch will deactivate your installation if it suspects you've got a pirated version." No benefit to the consumer at all. In fact, it's arguably just flat-out anti-consumer - a pirate can just check the box off to not install it, and it being run on a regular consumer machine carries nothing but a risk of the OS being deactivated unjustly.

Another example: driver updates that end up destroying hardware because the company that shipped the driver update suspects you're using a counterfeit chip, with Microsoft not giving a fuck as to what this does to the computer used by the unsuspecting customer (who might very well be using the computer to do something rather critical).

This already happened with Windows 7: http://www.zdnet.com/article/ftdi-admits-to-bricking-innocent-users-chips-in-silent-update/

And they did it again with Windows 10: http://hackaday.com/2016/02/01/ftdi-drivers-break-fake-chips-again/

The second time around didn't outright brick the chips, but it wrote illegitimate data to the chip, and there's no way to know what impact that might have on some devices.

Unfortunately, this is just the tip of the iceberg for what's in store for us as companies get a tighter and tighter grip on computing devices. Quite frankly, we ain't seen nothin' yet.
